title: Design Twitter Feed
pattern: hash set + bounded min-heap (top-k over an ordered log)
statement:
You are building the read path of a Twitter-like service. The log `tweets` records every post in chronological order: `tweets[i]` carries a post as `[authorId, tweetId, ...]`, and a smaller index means an older post. Only the first two entries of a row are read, so a row that does not carry both an author id and a tweet id is not a post. `follows` lists follow relations as rows `[followerId, followeeId, ...]`, again reading only the first two entries of a row, and the same relation may be listed more than once; a row that does not name both ids states no relation.

Return the home feed of `userId`: the tweet ids of the 10 most recent posts written by `userId` or by any account that `userId` follows, ordered from newest to oldest. Return every matching tweet id when there are fewer than 10, and an empty list when nothing matches at all. A user's own posts always belong to their own feed, and every index of `tweets` is a distinct moment in time, so no two returned tweets tie.

Constraints: `1 <= tweets.length <= 200`, `0 <= follows.length <= 200`, `0 <= follows[i][j] <= 50`, `1 <= tweets[i][j] <= 10000`, `1 <= userId <= 50`.

constraints: Function signature: `function solve(follows: number[][], tweets: number[][], userId: number)`.
Inputs are JSON-serializable values satisfying the bounds stated above.
hints: Decide first which authors belong in the feed: the queried user plus everyone they follow. A hash set turns that membership test into a constant-time lookup.
The log already arrives in time order, so a full sort of every matching position is more work than the answer needs. Ask which end of the log holds the tweets you want.
To keep only the 10 newest matches in one pass, hold the candidates in a min-heap keyed by time and pop the smallest whenever the heap grows past 10.

editorial.approach: The brute force first collects the accounts the queried user follows in a hash set, then walks the whole log and records every index whose author is the user or a followed account, sorts those indices from newest to oldest and keeps the first 10, which costs O(n log n) time. The optimal solution walks the log once and feeds each match into a min-heap keyed by log index; whenever the heap grows past 10 entries the oldest index is popped, so the heap always holds exactly the 10 newest matches and is drained in order at the end, costing O(n log 10) time with a fixed extra space of 10 entries.
editorial.why_optimal: The log has to be read at least once because the 10 newest matches can sit anywhere in it, and only the 10 largest indices are ever needed, which a 10-element heap provides at a constant log 10 per step. The sort in the brute force pays for ordering every match, including the ones that are then thrown away, and with n capped at 200 that difference is small on the judge but real in reasoning: the heap never holds more than 10 items, so its memory does not grow with the input.
editorial.pitfalls: Leaving the user's own tweets out of the feed. Reading a row as a pair without checking its width first: rows are id lists of any length and only the first two entries name a post or a follow, so a short row has to be skipped instead of indexed. Double-counting a followee when the follow list repeats a pair, which is why matching is done per log position and not per followee. Pushing into the heap and trimming only at the end, which lets an old tweet outlive a newer one. Sorting the answer by tweet id rather than by recency.
